passage: Thomas leaned on the counter of the bookshop and said to Joseph, "I taught after college too, and I nearly ruined my degree. Then I made a rule. Ten hours a week, no more. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, six to eight, and Saturday morning. I wrote it on the wall calendar in red. Exam weeks stayed clear, all of them. If a parent asked for an extra class, I said, 'Sorry, that slot is not mine.' It felt hard the first month. After that it was easy." Thomas straightened a pile of books. "The money kept coming, and my studies were never eaten up. A boundary is just a decision you make once, so you don't have to make it every day."

qa.q: How many hours a week did Thomas allow for paid work?
qa.a: Thomas allowed ten hours a week.

qa.q: What did Thomas feel in the first month of the rule?
qa.a: Thomas felt uncomfortable holding the rule in the first month, as it felt hard, but after that it became easy.

qa.q: What could Joseph do to set a personal limit, and why?
qa.a: Joseph could write a personal weekly limit on a wall calendar and mark exam weeks clear, since a written rule is easier to keep.

qa.q: How might a parent who wanted an extra class have seen Thomas's answer?
qa.a: The parent may have felt disappointed but also learned that the slots were fixed, which makes future requests clearer.

grounding: An elder recalls limiting paid work to ten hours a week in fixed evening slots and keeping exam weeks free.

passage:
Anirban edited wedding videos for a small studio run by Lakshmi, and the work never ran out. In his first month he worked whenever files arrived, sometimes till 2 a.m., and slept through two morning lectures.
So he set it down in steps. First, he blocked Monday to Friday, 7 to 9 p.m., on the calendar pinned above his desk: ten hours a week, no more. Second, he marked his three weeks of semester exams in red, with no editing at all. Third, he told Lakshmi the plan before the wedding season began.
The test came in November. Lakshmi's biggest client wanted a video early, in the very week of his first exam. She called on a Tuesday. 'Just this once, the weekend?'
Anirban looked at the red week. 'Not this week. I can start Monday, 7 p.m.'
Lakshmi sighed, but moved the client's date. By December his lab reports were on time again.

qa.q: Which hours did Anirban block for editing?
qa.a: Monday to Friday, 7 to 9 p.m., ten hours a week.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been worried about when Lakshmi asked for the weekend?
qa.a: He was likely anxious about losing the studio's goodwill, yet more worried about giving up his exam week, so he held the line politely.

qa.q: What else could help Anirban keep the slots from creeping?
qa.a: Agreeing delivery dates with Lakshmi well in advance, so rush requests are rarer and the ten-hour limit is easier to keep.

qa.q: How does the time limit look to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi finds it inconvenient during a rush and sighs, but gets a clear, predictable schedule from Anirban in return.

grounding: Shows a student limiting paid editing to ten hours in fixed evening slots and keeping exam weeks free, even under client pressure.

passage:
The shutter of Kamal's printing shop in Lajpat Nagar came down at nine, and for Hemant that used to mean nothing: he'd stay till eleven if orders piled up. Then his second-semester results came, and he dropped a grade in two subjects.
On Sunday he sat with Kamal over chai and made an offer. 'Tuesday to Saturday, six to eight. Ten hours, no more. And in exam months I don't come at all.' He wrote the slots on the whiteboard behind the counter, next to the order list.
Kamal frowned. 'Diwali cards come in October.'
'Then I'll take the Diwali rush in the second week, before my internals start.'
The first month was hard; twice Hemant walked out at eight with a stack still waiting. But in May he sat his exams without a single shift, and his marks climbed back.

qa.q: Which days and hours did Hemant offer to work?
qa.a: Tuesday to Saturday, six to eight.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel walking out at eight with a stack still waiting?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and uneasy leaving work undone, but determined to keep the limit he had set.

qa.q: What else could Hemant and Kamal agree on to make busy seasons easier?
qa.a: They could plan big orders like the Diwali cards ahead, so the rush falls in Hemant's free weeks instead of stretching his evenings.

qa.q: What is it like for Kamal when the slots are fixed?
qa.a: Kamal loses the late, flexible help he was used to and worries about the Diwali rush, but can plan around a helper who is predictable.

grounding: Shows a student fixing paid work at ten hours a week in set evening slots, with exam months kept free.
